Legs.Subject: the constructor and Bits round trip over the whole sixty-four-bit carrier: every swept raw, reinterpreted unchanged, reads back bit-for-bit
characteristic two, stated three ways at every swept operand: unary minus is the identity map, a polynomial added to itself is zero, and subtraction IS addition — the type's whole additive contract

the five declared constants read into locals before comparison so the run makes the comparison rather than the compiler: Zero equals AdditiveIdentity equals default with Bits zero, IsZero true, IsOne false and Degree −1; One equals MultiplicativeIdentity with Bits one, IsOne true and Degree zero; Indeterminate has Bits two and Degree one. A swap of any two of them reddens here
Zero is the two-sided identity for both + and − at every swept operand, and commutativity and associativity of + hold over three distinct operands

Legs.Subject: the checked operator's OVERFLOW PREDICATE (BinaryPolynomial.cs:88-94)

Legs.Subject: op_Multiply and op_CheckedMultiply at the four sixty-four-by-sixty-four reference operand pairs

Legs.Subject: the truncating product IS multiplication in GF(2)[t]/(t⁶⁴) — discarding every coefficient above degree 63 is reduction modulo t⁶⁴, a genuine ring quotient and not a lossy clamp — so commutativity, associativity and distributivity over + hold BIT-FOR-BIT at every swept operand including the ones that truncate. That is the statement which makes the type's truncation contract a ring rather than an accident

One is a two-sided multiplicative identity, Zero a two-sided annihilator, and multiplication by the Indeterminate is the single left shift, at every swept operand. ENVELOPE: the last of these is stated at degree 63 too, where BOTH sides truncate identically, so it pins agreement of the two truncations rather than an untruncated product
the value the checked operator returns when it does not throw
Legs.Against: the value operator * returns on the same operands
Legs.Shared: BinaryFieldKernels.CarrylessMultiply64 — the IDENTICAL member on both sides, called once per operator (BinaryPolynomial.cs:82 against 89), so the two cannot disagree about the product and only the reporting differs
Legs.Citation: the classical leg above, in this same case, which pins that shared kernel's low limb against Oracles.CarrylessProduct on the same operand stream

Legs.Subject: BinaryPolynomial.DivRem — top-down long division, aligning the divisor's leading term against the running remainder's and clearing one high coefficient per step (BinaryPolynomial.cs:195-212)
Legs.Against: Oracles.BinaryPolynomialDivRem — the BOTTOM-UP monomial route, which carries the pair (t^i div d, t^i mod d) forward one exponent at a time and sums the pairs at the dividend's set bits, never inspecting the dividend's leading term at all. Two different derivations of the same unique pair; EXACT on both sides, so the substrate condition does not arise. ENVELOPE on the operand stream: a zero divisor divides nothing, so a drawn zero divisor is replaced by One — applied IDENTICALLY in the subject and in the oracle — and the zero divisor's own contract is the refusal leg below

Legs.Subject: the division identity, at every swept pair: (quotient · divisor) + remainder is the dividend BIT-FOR-BIT. ENVELOPE, stated rather than implied: the product here is exact only because deg(quotient) + deg(divisor) equals deg(dividend), which is at most 63 — the identity leans on the truncating operator NOT truncating on these operands, and polynomial.multiply-vs-carryless-oracle is where the truncation itself is pinned
the remainder's degree is strictly below the divisor's at every swept pair, which is the half of Euclidean division the identity alone does not force

the refusal contract: DivRem, operator / and operator % each throw DivideByZeroException against the zero polynomial, checked at every swept dividend INCLUDING the zero one, where a guard that tested the dividend instead would pass unnoticed

the four poles: the zero dividend gives (Zero, Zero); a divisor of strictly higher degree gives (Zero, dividend) with no loop iteration at all; a non-zero polynomial divided by itself gives (One, Zero); and division by One gives (dividend, Zero) — the degenerate cases the sampled stream reaches only by accident
BinaryPolynomial.operator / and operator %
Legs.Against: DivRem's Quotient and Remainder
Legs.Shared: DivRem itself — both operators are one call through to it (BinaryPolynomial.cs:100-108), so agreement proves the projection and never the division
Legs.Citation: the classical leg above, in this same case, on the same operand stream: the pair the two operators project out of is pinned against Oracles.BinaryPolynomialDivRem before either operator reads it

Legs.Subject: BinaryPolynomial.GreatestCommonDivisor — the classical Euclidean loop, one long division per step through operator % (BinaryPolynomial.cs:216-223)
Legs.Against: Oracles.BinaryPolynomialGcd — the BINARY (Stein) descent, which performs no division anywhere: it strips the common power of t, then repeatedly exclusive-ors the lower-degree operand into the higher and strips the ts that exclusive or creates. Different algorithm, different primitives, same theorem; EXACT on both sides, so the substrate condition does not arise

Legs.Subject: the divisor DIVIDES both operands, at every swept pair and at the planted common-factor pair, checked through operator % against a zero remainder

MAXIMALITY, which divisibility alone does not force: the planted factor divides both operands by construction, so it is required to divide the REPORTED divisor. A routine that returned some common divisor rather than the greatest satisfies the divisibility leg and fails this one

the descent is actually exercised: each step plants a third drawn polynomial as a common factor of both operands, folded to One where either product would leave the carrier, because two random sixty-four-bit polynomials are coprime with high probability and a sweep of drawn pairs alone would spend nearly every case on the trivial answer. The planted case additionally requires the reported divisor's degree to reach the planted factor's

the poles the doc states: a zero operand returns the other, two zeros return zero, an operand against itself returns itself, an operand against One returns One, and the result is symmetric in its arguments

MONICITY is automatic here and the law says why: over the two-element field every non-zero polynomial has leading coefficient one, so the doc's 'monic gcd' costs no normalization step and there is no normalization to get wrong. The leading coefficient is asserted anyway, so a reader is not left looking for a missing check
BinaryPolynomial.operator << at every ladder count through 63 (BinaryPolynomial.cs:114-122)
Legs.Against: the low sixty-four coefficients of Oracles.CarrylessProduct against the monomial t^count — multiplication by a monomial derived independently of any shift. EXACT on both sides, so the substrate condition does not arise

Legs.Subject: BinaryPolynomial.operator >>> at every ladder count through 63 (BinaryPolynomial.cs:135-141)
Legs.Against: Oracles.BinaryPolynomialDivRem's quotient by the monomial t^count, the bottom-up monomial route — division by a monomial derived independently of any shift

Legs.Subject: the carrier-masking seam, from BOTH sides and by value: at count 63 the operator uses the carrier's own shift, and at counts 64, 65, 127 and int.MaxValue BOTH shifts return the zero polynomial rather than the carrier's masked result, which would wrap the count back into range and resurrect exactly the coefficients the operator promises to discard. A guard written as ≤ instead of < reddens at the 63 row and one written as < instead of ≤ at the 64 row
operator >> and operator >>> agree at every ladder count and every swept operand, which is the doc's claim that the two are one operation
the shifts round trip where nothing is lost: shifting up by a count and back down recovers the operand bit-for-bit whenever the operand's degree plus the count stays inside the carrier

the refusal ladder: all three shift operators throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming the 'count' parameter at −1, −64 and int.MinValue. operator >> reaches its guard through operator >>>, so the name it reports is the one the delegated-to operator captured, and the law asserts the NAME rather than merely that something threw
the shifts read as monomial multiplication and division
Legs.Against: BinaryPolynomial.operator * and operator / against the monomial t^count — two independently authored SHIPPED kernels that share no member with the shift operators, which is why this is an in-tree-independent leg and not a shared-substrate one: the shifts are plain carrier shifts behind a count guard (BinaryPolynomial.cs:114-141), the product routes to BinaryFieldKernels.CarrylessMultiply64 (cs:81-82) and the quotient to DivRem (cs:100-101)
Legs.Citation: polynomial.multiply-vs-carryless-oracle and polynomial.divrem-vs-monomial-oracle, which pin the product and the Euclidean pair classically; this leg then says the shifts agree with them, which the two classical legs above do NOT say on their own

Legs.Subject: the exhaustive count of monic irreducible polynomials at every degree 1 through 12
Legs.Against: Subjects.BinaryIrreducibleCounts — the first terms 2, 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, 30, 56, 99, 186, 335

Legs.Subject: BinaryPolynomial.IsIrreducible at EVERY monic polynomial of degree 1 through 8, both constant terms — 510 decisions
Legs.Against: Oracles.BinaryPolynomialIsIrreducible, exhaustive trial division by every monic polynomial of degree one through half the subject's, which is the DEFINITION. The subject's route is Ben-Or/Rabin — repeated Frobenius exponentiation and gcd inside BinaryFieldKernels — so the two share no procedure at all. This is the per-polynomial statement the census cannot make: an aggregate count is satisfied by a false positive paired with a false negative, and this leg is not. EXACT on both sides, so the substrate condition does not arise

Legs.Subject: IsIrreducible on products the ORACLE constructed, at degrees up to 63
Legs.Against: Oracles.CarrylessProduct of two polynomials each of degree at least one — a product of two non-constant factors is reducible by definition, so the reference verdict is derived without consulting the subject and without any decision procedure at all. One-sided but COMPLETE, and it is the only independent statement this campaign can make above the trial-division ceiling; the pairs reach degrees 40, 48, 55 and 63

Legs.Subject: IsIrreducible at the degree-8, degree-16 and degree-32 canonical moduli
Legs.Against: Subjects.BinaryCatalogModuli — t⁸+t⁴+t³+t+1, t¹⁶+t⁵+t³+t+1 and t³²+t⁷+t³+t²+1, all required irreducible

The indeterminate t is the row that separates the second rule from the third — it is irreducible AND has a zero constant term — and the law asserts it explicitly
IsIrreducible above degree one with a non-zero constant term

Legs.Subject: BinaryPolynomial.IsPrimitive at EVERY monic polynomial with a non-zero constant term of degree 1 through 10 — 1023 decisions (BinaryPolynomial.cs:261-299)
Legs.Against: Oracles.BinaryPolynomialIsPrimitive, which computes the EXACT multiplicative order of t: the least divisor of 2^d − 1 at which t^e is one, over EVERY divisor rather than only the maximal prime quotients, with the divisors coming from its own trial-division factorization rather than from UnsignedNumberFunctions.EnumeratePrimeFactors, and with NO irreducibility decision anywhere — an order of exactly 2^d − 1 forces irreducibility by itself, since that many distinct powers in a ring of 2^d elements leaves no non-unit. The subject decides irreducibility first through BinaryField<ulong>, then tests only t^((2^d−1)/p) for the prime divisors p, and returns a boolean. Different criterion, different factorization, different arithmetic; EXACT on both sides, so the substrate condition does not arise

Legs.Subject: the COUNT of primitive polynomials at each degree 1 through 10
Legs.Against: the closed form φ(2^d − 1)/d, with the totient formed in the claim body by its own trial division rather than by the shipped prime-factor enumerator the subject uses — the classical census to degree 14. What THIS case adds over an aggregate census is the per-polynomial leg above: an aggregate count is satisfied by a false positive paired with a false negative, and a per-polynomial order is not

Legs.Subject: IsPrimitive at the two witnesses that separate primitivity from irreducibility
Legs.Against: t + 1 primitive; t⁴+t³+t²+t+1 irreducible and NOT primitive, with the oracle's order exactly 5
Legs.Citation: hand-derived: t + 1 is DigitalNetSampler.PlaneGenerator, the smallest primitive polynomial there is, and t⁵ + 1 = (t + 1)(t⁴+t³+t²+t+1) puts the root's order at 5 rather than at 2⁴ − 1 = 15. The same negative witness is what Post's digital-net stage uses (DigitalNetStage.cs:113-117)

Legs.Subject: primitivity is strictly stronger than irreducibility, checked in both directions across the whole census: every primitive polynomial is irreducible, and the degree-4 witness is irreducible while not primitive, so the implication is asserted rather than assumed and its converse is refuted by a named row. The census additionally requires that no polynomial the subject calls non-primitive has t at the full order

the degree cap, from BOTH sides and through the declared constant read into a local: MaximumPrimitiveDegree is 32, degree-32 polynomials are decided without throwing, and a degree-33 polynomial throws NotSupportedException. The constant is read into a local before comparison so the run makes the comparison rather than the compiler folding it away
IsPrimitive over a hoisted ladder of UNLABELLED polynomials at degrees 16, 24 and 32
Legs.Against: Oracles.BinaryPolynomialIsPrimitive's order at the same rows. The rows carry no claimed verdict — the oracle is the judge — so no transcription mistake in the table can make this case red at landing, and the statement is still the full one: the subject's boolean must equal the oracle's. Both arms ARE reached above the census ceiling, and the claim body ASSERTS that rather than resting on the table as it stands today: it counts the accepting and the rejecting rows PER DEGREE and returns a named counterexample if 16, 24 or 32 ever stops carrying one. Each degree carries the first primitive polynomial deep.polynomial-primitive-order-and-census's own search reaches, beside a catalog modulus and the reducible t^d + 1. The counters are not decoration — this is the only Default-tier evidence that IsPrimitive's ACCEPTING arm works above degree 10, since the exhaustive census stops there and the searching mirror is Deep-only, and a ladder that drifted to all-rejecting rows would satisfy a row-by-row comparison while proving nothing about that arm

Legs.Subject: IsPrimitive on the indeterminate t — the ONE polynomial in the whole type the constant-term gate has to answer by itself — returns FALSE (BinaryPolynomial.cs:271). The law asserts alongside it that t is still reported irreducible, which is what makes it the unique operand reaching that gate: every other zero-constant-term polynomial has degree at least two and IsIrreducible refuses it first, so a change that made t reducible would leave the gate unreached and this row decorative
Legs.Against: Oracles.BinaryPolynomialIsPrimitive at t, which agrees and adds the reason: no divisor of 2^1 − 1 = 1 sends t to one, because t reduces to 0 modulo t and every power of it is 0, so the exact order is not merely short — it does not exist. The oracle takes no irreducibility decision anywhere and never builds a quotient, where the subject's answer comes from a constant-term test in front of one. The conventional answer too: a primitive polynomial has a non-zero constant term. EXACT on both sides, so the substrate condition does not arise

Legs.Subject: ENVELOPE on a line no operand can falsify: the prime-group-order fallback (BinaryPolynomial.cs:292), which supplies the group order as its own only prime divisor, is a mathematical no-op. Where 2^d − 1 is prime every irreducible polynomial IS primitive, and the single test it adds is t^1 ≠ 1, which holds for every modulus except t + 1 — whose group order is 1 and which never reaches the fallback. No sweep and no census can distinguish its presence from its absence, and the campaign states that rather than implying the line is covered
the DEGREES of BinaryPolynomial.FactorOddCycle's output at each ladder order (BinaryPolynomial.cs:151-189)
Legs.Against: Oracles.BinaryCyclotomicFactorDegrees — the orbit sizes of x ↦ 2x on Z/nZ. The classical structure of t^n − 1 over GF(2): the Frobenius map permutes the n-th roots of unity by squaring and each orbit is the root set of one irreducible factor. NO polynomial is multiplied, divided or reduced anywhere in that computation, where the subject enumerates monic candidates, tests each for irreducibility and divides — the two sides could not fail together. EXACT on both sides, so the substrate condition does not arise

Legs.Subject: the VALUES of the returned factors
Legs.Against: their fold under Oracles.CarrylessProduct, required to be exactly t^n + 1 in BigInteger. The re-multiplication is done by the ORACLE rather than by BinaryPolynomial.operator *, which is what separates this leg from integer.symmetry-lattice-exact-structure's re-multiplication of SymmetryLattice.RayCycleFactors. That statement declares itself shared-substrate:delegation-twin precisely BECAUSE the same type produces the factors and multiplies them back, so a shared error would cancel there, and it cites this leg for the property itself

Legs.Subject: each returned factor's irreducibility
Legs.Against: Oracles.BinaryPolynomialIsIrreducible, exhaustive trial division — so the claim that the factors are irreducible is judged without running the subject's own decision a second time. The deepest row the Default ladder hands it is degree 8

Legs.Subject: the factors are pairwise DISTINCT, each is monic and each has a non-zero constant term, which together with the degree multiset and the exact re-multiplication is the whole factorization: t^n + 1 is squarefree for odd n — its formal derivative is t^(n−1), which shares no factor with it — so 'distinct' is the right contract and a repeated factor would mean the quotient loop divided one out twice

the declared ORDER: ascending by degree, then ascending by packed value. Order 15 is the row that makes the tie-break observable at all, with three factors of degree 4. ENVELOPE, stated rather than implied: the discovery order is ALREADY ascending in both keys — degrees are tried upward and candidates within a degree are enumerated upward — so removing either sort key leaves the output unchanged and this leg cannot falsify their presence, only their inversion

the refusal ladder: 0, −1, 32, 33, int.MinValue, int.MaxValue and every even order in [2, 30] each throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming the 'cycleOrder' parameter, and order 1 returns exactly the single factor t + 1

ENVELOPE on an unreachable branch: the InvalidOperationException at BinaryPolynomial.cs:180-183 — 'the binary factorization did not finish with an irreducible factor' — cannot fire for any legal order. The loop divides out every factor of degree at most n/2, so the leftover is a product of factors each of degree above n/2 whose degrees sum to at most n, which admits exactly one factor. No operand reaches it, and the campaign says so instead of implying the branch is covered. Order 17 is the ladder row that would reach it if the outer loop bound were narrowed by one, which is what makes that row load-bearing rather than decorative
